title: High and low notes, embouchure and proving himself on stage
summary: Pedal tones and range, a dance at Streeter where a high school band watched him, and a tavern on State Street where an army trombonist doubted him.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Did you ever use pedal tones much on trombone?
Oh, yes, I had a good ambusho. At one time, I could hit the highest note and drop down below, below the ground.
I used to practice that, see, because that's what they used to have said.

Oh, you can make high notes, but you can't make no low notes. And some father said, well, you can make low notes, and you can't make no high, see. So I fought hard to get both, see. And sometimes I would catch myself and be playing a melody or something like that, and make that high note and drop down. And I noticed that, you know. I'd say, no, that's easier to do. If you get the ambusho for it, you know, you can do it just, look like, without the least effort, see. We played a dance once. We played a dance over in, uh, Streeter. You know, Streeter, Illinois. Yeah. And there was a high school band that was playing there. We was playing. I was playing with a fellow by the name of Oscar Young. We played over there in the park. They give us some nice park, the band, the brass band was playing over on one side, and we was playing on the other side. Before we got through playing the man, the professor had them all the way watching me. I said, what the world of them guys? They're watching you, see.
I said, well, I'll just go to the ground.
go ahead now and try not to make too many mistakes.

Because he was listening. They're teachers. This man was teaching these young fellas, and they had a big band. And he was telling them, I could see him telling them something. I don't know what he was telling them. He was telling them something. And they stood there, and those guys stayed right around me. I kind of felt embarrassed, you know. But they never heard the trombone thing. That was the trombone they ever heard. So that was one of my attempts to find out whether I was good or not. And after we come back in Chicago, we played at Deluxe. The upstairs had a, what do you call it? Taverns then? Yeah. We played up there. Was that on State Street? On State and 35th. There was a fellow come from the Army. He'd come in. First man he started picking there was me. Where did you get this guy? I said, he's tough. He said, what's, what's your, how long have you been playing? I said, oh, just a couple of months. He said, you can't fool me with that. He said, you don't need to think you're fooling me with that. He said, I'm a trombone player myself. I didn't say no more. Well, you see, it's something, I don't know, it's something different. I'm not saying bragging on my trombone playing, but it's something different because when I play around places, before I get through, the whole gang is right up there in front of me. And the other fellas, they ain't paying so much attention, but they're watching me, see. And we had, we had a very good band. This Paul Barberine, he played with us for a while. I know him. He's a nice little drummer. And he didn't stay in Chicago long. He only stayed a while. But he was very good. But Baby Dots is just about as good a drummer as a man wants for strict time. Yeah, I think so. Yeah, he's as good a drummer as a man wants. He'll hold a time. Time. He gets a tempo. He's got it. All those boys that played, there was none of them that I could play with. You know, I played all of them, but they're so easy to play with Dots. I think he played with you with Hightower's band
